scenes.text: The first big video game hit broke down because it was too full of money.
In nineteen seventy-two, a brand new company called Atari was started by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney.
They hired a young engineer named Allan Alcorn.
As a training exercise, Bushnell asked him to build a simple ping-pong game.
Alcorn even made its famous beep sounds from tones already inside the circuit.
The result was Pong, and it was so fun they built a coin-operated cabinet.
In late summer, they put the prototype in Andy Capp's Tavern, a bar in Sunnyvale, California.
It was just a small black-and-white TV inside a hand-painted cabinet.
A few weeks later, the bar called to say the machine was broken.
When Alcorn opened it up, the coin box was jammed full of quarters.
He later said he was scooping out fistfuls of them.
On November twenty-ninth, nineteen seventy-two, Atari announced Pong cabinets for the rest of the country.
Atari eventually sold about thirty-five thousand of them.
Pong helped kick off the whole video game industry.
Would you have paid a quarter to play Pong? Tell me below.

title: This video game broke because it was too full of money 🕹️
caption: Atari's first Pong cabinet, tested in a Sunnyvale bar in 1972, stopped working because its coin box was jammed with quarters. Atari went on to sell about 35,000 of them.
